title: Acceptance and rising spirits
hook: bhaana and chardi kala belong together

segments.voice: Yesterday, chardi kala as philosophy: the tree on the windy hill, held by its roots. Your line was rising, rooted. Which setback did you meet with a small smile? Day one thousand four hundred six.

Two words have been walking through this stretch of the path. Bhaana, the will, the sweet acceptance of what the Lord sends. And chardi kala, rising spirits. Set them side by side and they can look like opposites. One bows its head; the other lifts it. Some people hear acceptance and think of giving up. Some hear rising spirits and think of fighting fate. The Sikh tradition doesn't choose between them. It says them in a single breath, at the very end of the Ardas. Today: how the two belong together.

First, the line. Yesterday's words again: Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhaane sarbat da bhala. Rising spirits, and then, by your will, the good of all. Rising and accepting share one sentence, and neither cancels the other. Second, a refrain. In the Japji, Guru Nanak stops at the end of a pauri, overwhelmed by the size of creation, and says, in paraphrase: whatever pleases you, that alone is good; you are forever whole, formless One. Jo tudh bhaavai saaee bhalee kaar. Then the next pauri ends with the same words, and the next. Acceptance there isn't a single grim moment. It's a line the Japji keeps coming back to. Third, what acceptance isn't. Bhaana doesn't mean liking injustice or sitting still. The same people who recite that refrain every morning run free kitchens and stand up to wrong. Acceptance is about the ground under your feet: this happened. Rising is about the next step: and now. Fourth, the hinge. Accept first, so your strength stops pouring into fighting what already is. Then rise, so it can pour into what can still be done. A farmer wakes to find hail has flattened the field. Bhaana says: it happened, and it's in the Lord's hands. Chardi kala says: there's seed in the shed. Grieve the field. Then replant. Accept, then rise.
screen: `ONE LINE OF THE ARDAS.` · `WHATEVER PLEASES YOU IS GOOD.` · `ACCEPTING ISN'T GIVING UP.` · `THE FARMER AFTER THE HAIL.` · then, large: `ACCEPT, THEN RISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: accept, then rise. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you can't change today: a loss, a diagnosis, a decision someone else made. On the next few breaths out, let it simply be true: this happened. No arguing with it. Then, on the breaths in, ask one quiet question: and now? Let one small next step show itself: a call, a meal, a walk, some rest. Accept on the out-breath. Rise on the in-breath. If you pray, you can hold the Japji's words in mind: jo tudh bhaavai saaee bhalee kaar. The bell holds the time.
Acceptance and rising spirits. Bhaana and chardi kala, said in one line of the Ardas: accept what has come, then rise toward what can be done. Today's word.
Your line: accept, then rise. Today, when something doesn't go your way, say it happened, out loud or inside, and then take one small step anyway. Day one thousand four hundred six.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of living in bhaana, God's will, while keeping chardi kala, rising spirits; the two are joined in the closing words of the Ardas, and the Japji's refrain 'jo tudh bhaavai saaee bhalee kaar' voices the acceptance.
